title: Tillage

definition.text: The preparation of soil for farming by mechanically agitating it, for example by digging, stirring or overturning it.

facts.text: Hand methods include shovelling, picking, mattock work, hoeing and raking; animal-drawn or machine work includes ploughing, rototilling, rolling, harrowing and cultivating.
Deeper, more thorough tillage is called primary and shallower, more selective tillage secondary; harrowing and rototilling often combine the two in one pass.
In farming, cultivation overlaps with tillage, but it can also mean shallow, selective secondary tillage of row crops that kills weeds while sparing the crop.
Tillage kills weeds by uprooting them or burying their leaves, which keeps them from competing with the crop and from setting seed.
In 1731 Jethro Tull argued that soil had to be pulverized into a fine powder for plants to feed on it, and that land could never be tilled too much.
Scientific observation has shown the opposite: tillage robs soil of the structure that lets roots, water and nutrients in, speeds erosion and compacts the soil.
Tilling the prairie topsoil of the American Midwest helped cause the Dust Bowl; in 2019 erosion in the United States still took an estimated 3 trillion pounds of soil.
Modern agricultural science has greatly reduced tillage: with herbicides, crops tolerant of packed soil and direct-seeding equipment, crops can be grown for years without it.

notes: Earliest plough evidence (c. 4000 BCE, S:66beaa94c16c) carries a [timeframe?] tag in the source; left out. The tillage-versus-earthworm volume figure is already in the pilot Tilth entry.

definition.text: The division of tillage into deeper, more thorough primary operations and shallower, often more selective secondary ones.

facts.text: Primary tillage, such as ploughing, loosens the soil and mixes in fertilizer or plant material, leaving a rough surface.
It usually follows the last harvest, when soil is wet enough to plough but still gives traction, and aims for soft soil to a reasonable depth, buried residues, killed weeds and aeration.
Secondary tillage is any later operation: it works in fertilizer, reduces soil to a finer tilth, levels the surface, shapes rows and controls weeds.
Its smoother surface finish is what many crops need for a good seedbed.
Seedbed tools include harrows, dibbles, hoes, shovels, rotary tillers, subsoilers, ridge- or bed-forming tillers, rollers and cultivators.
Weed control by tillage usually uses cultivators or hoes that disturb only the top few centimetres of soil around the crop plants.

title: Intensive tillage

definition.text: Tillage that leaves less than 15% crop residue cover, or less than 500 pounds per acre (560 kg/ha) of small grain residue, on the soil.

facts.text: It often involves several passes with implements such as a mouldboard, disk or chisel plough, then a finisher with a harrow, rolling basket and cutter to prepare the seedbed.
It is often called conventional tillage, but in the United States conservation tillage is now more widely used, so the label is often inappropriate.
Conventional tillage means the operations standard for a place and crop, which tend to bury residues; it is the baseline for costing erosion control practices.
Faster travel with disks and chisel ploughs, and steeper disk angles, bury more residue and so make tillage more intensive.

notes: Folds in the one-sentence Conventional tillage page (S:963d60997d43).

definition.text: Tillage that leaves 15 to 30% crop residue cover, or 500 to 1000 pounds per acre (560 to 1100 kg/ha) of small grain residue, during the critical erosion period.

facts.text: It may use a chisel plough, field cultivators or other implements.
Tillage systems are compared by percentage residue because the amount of crop residue left on the surface affects soil loss by erosion.

definition.text: A group of practices that reduce tillage and leave at least 30% of crop residue, or at least 1,000 lb/ac (1,100 kg/ha) of small grain residue, on the surface during the critical erosion period.

facts.text: The residue slows water movement and softens raindrop impact on soil particles, so less soil erodes.
Fewer passes over the field save fuel and labour and reduce soil compaction; it also benefits predatory arthropods that can help control pests.
Its forms include no-till, strip-till, mulch-till, ridge-till and rotational tillage, in which soil is tilled every two years or less often.
It is used on over 370 million acres, mostly in South America, Oceania and North America, and in most years since 1997 it has covered more US cropland than intensive or reduced tillage.
By 2014 more than 75% of cropland on the Canadian Prairies had adopted conservation tillage.
Researchers found a nearly 60 percent reduction in runoff losses under conservation tillage, which also guards the surface against crusting.
Less exposed dark soil means slower warming in spring, which delays planting of the next corn crop.
Equipment designed to cut water erosion may not reduce tillage erosion.

verification.title: Conservation tillage mitigates the negative effect of landscape simplification on biological control
verification.evidence: Conservation tillage was found to support more abundant predator communities and higher aphid predation (16% higher than in the fields managed under conventional tillage).
verification.note: the paper's 16% is higher aphid predation; the entry gives adoption (75%) and runoff reduction (60%)

definition.text: The consequences of tilling for a soil: it loosens and aerates the topsoil for planting, but it also degrades structure, speeds erosion and compacts the soil.

facts.text: Benefits include loosening and aerating the A horizon, mixing residue, humus and nutrients evenly into the soil, and destroying weeds mechanically.
Autumn tillage lets frost crumble the exposed soil over winter, giving a smooth surface for spring planting.
Tillage can reduce slugs, cutworms, armyworms and other pests drawn to old residues, and crop diseases harboured in surface residues.
Drying the soil before seeding appears both as a benefit, in wetter climates, and as a drawback.
Tilled soil loses nutrients and water-storing ability, and its infiltration rate falls, so more water runs off and erodes it.
Tillage breaks the cohesion between particles and destroys aggregates, and it reduces organic matter and soil life such as microbes, earthworms and ants.
It disrupts the hyphal network of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, lowering the soil's capacity to infect new roots.
Other harms are compaction into a tillage pan, chemical runoff and eutrophication of waters fed by nutrient runoff.

sources.title: 3.3: Human Influences - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

title: Plough pan

definition.text: A compacted layer of soil created by tillage, also called a tillage pan.

facts.text: Over-ploughing can form a hardpan, which farmers usually break with a subsoiler that slices through the hardened layer deep below the surface.
Chisel ploughs and zone tillage are used to break up plough pans.
Continued cultivation and traffic create compacted, impermeable layers within the soil profile.

notes: No article of its own; passes the 2+ pages test (Tillage, Plough, Soil structure). Close to the man-made hardpans of the Hardpan entry (horizons chapter): merge there if selection prefers.

definition.text: The damage tilling does to buried ancient remains such as long barrows.

facts.text: In the UK, half of the long barrows in Gloucestershire and almost all the burial mounds in Essex have been damaged.
English Heritage reported in 2003 that powerful modern tractors had done as much damage in six decades as traditional farming in the previous six centuries.

definition.text: Any of the treatments applied to a forest site to ready it for seeding or planting.

facts.text: It aims to ease regeneration by improving access, reducing or rearranging slash, and ameliorating poor forest floor, soil or vegetation conditions.
In Ontario around 1970 the most widely used technique was mechanical scarification with bulldozer-mounted blades, rakes, V-ploughs or teeth, or tractor-drawn scarifiers.
In a British Columbia disk-trenching trial, trees on south-, east- and west-facing microsites had larger tenth-year stem volumes than north-facing or untreated ones.
Choosing the planting spot mattered more overall than the orientation of the trench.

title: Slash burning for site preparation

definition.text: Broadcast or prescribed burning of logging slash on cleared forest sites to prepare them for planting or seeding.

facts.text: Burning raises soil pH, by as much as 2 units, a 100-fold change, and the increase persisted more than a year in central British Columbia.
The higher pH may explain copper and iron deficiencies in white spruce foliage on burned clearcuts.
Phosphorus availability rose after one burn and was still higher 21 months later, but in another study it fell below pre-burn levels within 9 months; nitrogen is lost.
Burns are patchy: in one 140-ha slash burn only 4% burned severely, 47% lightly and 49% not at all.

notes: The two phosphorus results come from different burns in the same zone, so they are stated as facts, not a conflict.

definition.text: A forest site-preparation treatment that builds raised planting spots, which have improved seedling performance on cold, wet sites.

facts.text: Mounds warmed fastest, averaging 10 and 7 °C warmer than the control at soil depths of 0.5 cm and 10 cm.
They reached a mean soil temperature of 10 °C at 10 cm depth 5 days after planting; the control took 58 days.
In the first growing season mounds had 3 times as many days with mean soil temperature above 10 °C as control microsites.
Mounds also received over 4 times the daily light energy reaching control microsites.

definition.text: A farm tool for loosening or turning over soil before sowing seed or planting.

facts.text: Ploughing chiefly turns over the uppermost soil, bringing fresh nutrients to the surface and burying weeds and crop remains to decay; the trenches it cuts are furrows.
Ploughing and cultivating even out the upper 12 to 25 centimetres (5 to 10 in) of soil, where most plant feeder roots grow.
A ploughed field is normally left to dry and then harrowed before planting.
Ploughs were first pulled by people, then by oxen, horses and mules, then by steam engines, and from the early 20th century by tractors.
The earliest ploughs had no wheels, a type the Romans called an aratrum; Celtic peoples first used wheeled ploughs in the Roman era.
A Sumerian poem from the 3rd millennium BC stages a debate between the hoe and the plough over which is better.
In 1837 John Deere began making polished steel ploughs strong enough to farm US soils, such as tough Midwest prairie, once thought unsuitable.
Where soil damage and erosion threaten, the traditional plough has given way to shallower ploughing or other conservation tillage.

definition.text: The early animal-drawn scratch plough, which drags a share through the topsoil to cut a shallow furrow.

facts.text: Domesticated oxen in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, perhaps as early as the 6th millennium BC, supplied the draft power that made the ard possible.
A ploughed field from about 2800 BCE has been found at Kalibangan, India.
Because it left undisturbed strips between furrows, fields were cross-ploughed both ways, which tended to form squarish Celtic fields.
It suits loamy or sandy soils renewed by floods, as in the Nile Delta and Fertile Crescent, and struggled in northern Europe's heavy soils.

definition.text: Turning soil with hand-held digging sticks and hoes, the way soil was worked when agriculture began.

facts.text: Hoes were used in very fertile areas such as the Nile banks, renewed by the annual flood, to cut furrows for seeds.
Digging sticks, hoes and mattocks arose in many places, and hoe cultivation must have been common wherever farming was practised.
Hoe farming is the traditional tillage of tropical and subtropical regions with stony soils, steep slopes, root crops and widely spaced coarse grains.

definition.text: A plough whose curved mould board lifts the slice of soil cut by the share and turns it over into the previous furrow.

facts.text: The coulter cuts down into the soil and the share cuts horizontally, freeing a strip of sod that rolls over and lands upside down.
General-purpose mould boards turn the slice gently for ploughing up to 200 mm deep; digger boards shatter it at 300 mm or more; semi-digger boards work at about 250 mm.
The heavy iron mouldboard plough was invented in Han China in the 1st and 2nd centuries and later spread to the Netherlands.
It greatly cut the time needed to prepare a field, and its ridges and furrows form channels that drain the soil.
Ploughing to 20 cm aerates the soil and works in residues, manure, lime and fertiliser, speeding mineralisation and cutting nitrogen loss by denitrification.
It raises numbers of soil-eating endogeic earthworms but deters vertical-burrowing anecic ones.
It leaves little surface residue against wind and water erosion, and over-ploughing can form a hardpan.
Being hard to turn, it changed fields from mostly square plots into long rectangular strips, hence the furlong.

definition.text: A wheeled plough heavy enough to carry a large metal-faced mould board and so to work the heavy soils of northern Europe.

facts.text: By the Han period Chinese ploughshares were wholly cast iron, the earliest known heavy iron mould-board ploughs.
Adoption of the carruca heavy plough in Europe accompanied the three-field system in the later 8th and early 9th centuries, raising yields per unit of land.
Pulling it took four to eight oxen, more than one peasant household had, so it made farming communal and helped the manorial system rise.
Heavy ploughs raised food production, coinciding with a marked rise in world population in the second millennium AD.

definition.text: A plough for deep tillage that loosens and aerates soil while leaving crop residue on the surface.

facts.text: Unlike most ploughs it does not invert the soil, which suits no-till and low-till farming; some consider it more sustainable than the mouldboard plough.
It can reduce the effects of compaction and help break up plough pans and hardpans.
It is essentially a heavy-duty field cultivator working 15 cm to 46 cm deep, needing 10 to 20 horsepower (7.5 to 14.9 kW) per shank.
Cultivator teeth work near the surface, mainly against weeds, whereas chisel shanks work deep, so cultivating needs far less power per shank.

sources.title: 16.2: Tillage Systems - Geosciences LibreTexts (Building Soils for Better Crops, 4th ed. (Magdoff and van Es))

title: Subsoiling

definition.text: Deep tillage with a subsoiler, an implement whose heavy shanks loosen and break up soil below the depth reached by ploughs, harrows or rototillers.

facts.text: Most tillage tools work the top 15–20 cm (6–8 in), while a subsoiler loosens soil to twice that depth, usually 45–75 cm (18–30 in) or more.
Angled wings on the shanks lift and shatter the hardpan that builds up through compaction, improving the growth of crops wherever compaction is a problem.
After subsoiling, roots reach deeper moisture and nutrients in hot, dry seasons, and in wet weather water drains through the shattered zones, so crops are less likely to drown.
It is slow and power-hungry: pulling one point through hard soil takes 60 to 100 horsepower (45 to 75 kW), and shanks should reach 2.5–5 cm (1–2 in) below the deepest compacted layer.
A subsoiler is not a mole plough, which cuts underground drainage channels.
The para-plough is a primary tillage implement that loosens compacted layers 3 to 4 dm (12 to 16 inches) deep without inverting soil, keeping surface residue high.
In-row subsoiling counts among the conservation tillage practices.
On poorly drained land deep tillage may substitute for costlier tile drainage, and subsoiling may be needed where a clay-enriched lower horizon becomes too compacted.

notes: Extended in gap-fill with the crawled Subsoiler page; also on Plough, Tillage, Lessivage and Nutrient management.

definition.text: A deep plough with a torpedo-shaped tip that leaves a drainage channel underground, or breaks up deep impermeable layers, without digging trenches.

facts.text: Its bullet-shaped share forms a tunnel about 75 mm (3.0 in) across, and an expander presses the soil outward into a long-lasting channel.
Mole drains lie up to 950 mm (37 in) deep at an angle to pipe drains, into which their water seeps and runs to a ditch.
A simple field test: if a pencil pushed through a hand-compacted, tennis-ball-sized sample from moling depth leaves the ball unsplit, the subsoil suits mole ploughing.
Heavy land needs draining to bring its water content down to a level efficient for plant growth.

definition.text: A farm implement for surface tillage, used after ploughing to break up and smooth the soil surface.

facts.text: Harrowing breaks up clods to give a tilth suitable for planting seeds; coarser harrowing can also remove weeds and cover seed after sowing.
Ploughs cut the upper 12 to 25 centimetres of soil and leave furrows, and cultivators disturb only narrow tracks between rows, whereas harrows disturb the whole surface.
The four general types are disc harrows, tine harrows (including spring-tooth, drag and spike harrows), chain harrows and chain-disk harrows.
Farmers commonly run a disk harrow first to slice the large clods left by the mouldboard plough, then a spring-tooth harrow, leaving a smooth field with powdery surface soil.
Chain harrows do light work such as levelling the tilth or covering seed, while disc harrows do heavy work such as breaking up sod after ploughing.
Where harrowing leaves a very fine tilth, or the soil is light enough to blow away, a roller is often added as the last implement.
A power harrow's tines spin on vertical axes, so unlike a rotary tiller it does not invert soil layers or slice the subsurface in a way that can form a hardpan.
In China the rake had developed into the harrow by the end of the Han dynasty, when the flat pa and the vertical chao were both known.

title: Cultivator

definition.text: A farm implement for secondary tillage, either a frame with teeth dragged through the soil or a machine with rotating disks or teeth such as a rotary tiller.

facts.text: Cultivators stir and pulverize soil before planting to aerate it and prepare a smooth, loose seedbed, or after crop emergence to kill weeds.
Unlike a harrow, which disturbs the whole soil surface, a cultivator disturbs soil in careful patterns that spare the crop plants.
Toothed cultivators resemble chisel ploughs, but their teeth work near the surface against weeds, while chisel shanks work deep to break hardened layers.
Field cultivators prepare the seedbed, bury residue to help warm the soil, control weeds and mix the soil so the crop has enough water and nutrients.

notes: Crawled page that no chapter's dossier lists; drafted here as a core tillage implement.

title: Seedbed

definition.text: The local soil environment into which seeds are planted.

facts.text: Seedbed soil needs to be loose and smooth, without large lumps, so seeds can be planted easily at the depth that germinates them best.
On farms it is usually prepared by secondary tillage with harrows and cultivators, perhaps after primary tillage with mouldboard or chisel ploughs; no-till skips this step.
Preparation breaks up compacted soil so air and water can enter and seedlings can penetrate; smaller seeds need a finer soil structure.
Organic matter such as compost or peat may be added to improve the seedbed's soil structure.

notes: Crawled page that no chapter's dossier lists; linked from the Tillage, Harrow and No-till farming blocks.

definition.text: A way of growing crops or pasture without disturbing the soil by tillage, also called zero tillage or direct drilling.

facts.text: It cuts tillage-caused erosion, especially on sandy, dry, sloping soils; the top inch of no-till soil holds more aggregates and is two to seven times less vulnerable than ploughed soil.
Surface residue helps rain and irrigation water infiltrate and limits evaporation; each tillage pass loses around 0.85 to 1.9 cm of water to evaporation.
Crops are sown into a herbicide-killed cover crop (sod seeding), through the previous crop's residue (direct seeding), or onto the bare surface (surface seeding).
No-till means never tilling a field; like strip tillage it is a form of conservation tillage, but the two terms are not equivalent.
Organized opposition to ploughing began in the 1940s with Edward H. Faulkner's Plowman's Folly, but trials spread only after post-war herbicides such as paraquat.
Land under no-till grew from about 45 million ha in 1999 to 72 million ha in 2003 and 111 million ha in 2009; in 2014 South America held 47% of it.
Light-coloured residue absorbs less solar energy than bare soil, so no-till soil warms and dries more slowly in spring, which may delay planting.
Nitrogen immobilized in decomposing residue often reduces yields and calls for more fertilizer, but after a transition (4–5 years in Kansas) soil organic matter may build up.

title: No-till and soil carbon

definition.text: The dispute over whether no-till farming really increases the organic carbon stored in soil.

facts.text: Many studies report more soil organic carbon under no-till, but others find the effect absent in some systems, depending on factors such as climate and topsoil carbon content.
Some question whether measured gains are real or artefacts of flawed testing methods or other factors.
A 2014 study found the no-till subsurface layer often loses more soil organic carbon over time than the surface gains, and called for a uniform definition of sequestration.
A 2020 study found no-till combined with cover cropping stores more carbon than either practice alone.
Critics add that no-till may increase herbicide use, diminishing or eliminating its carbon benefits.
No-till cuts emissions of nitrous oxide, a gas 300 times stronger than CO2 that lasts 120 years, by 40–70% depending on rotation.
The cooling from no-till croplands' higher albedo is similar in magnitude to other biogeochemical carbon sequestration processes.

contested_note: Sources dispute whether the soil carbon gains measured under no-till are real and general, or offset by losses deeper in the profile.

definition.text: Controlling weeds without tillage, using herbicides, cover crops, mowing or crimping in place of cultivation.

facts.text: Herbicides such as glyphosate replace tillage for seedbed preparation, so no-till uses more herbicide than conventional tillage.
Residue left on the surface can bring different, greater or more frequent disease and weed problems than tilled fields.
Weed-suppressing cover crops add organic residue but must be killed, typically by crimping at flowering, and the crop is planted through the remaining mulch.
Herbicides are not strictly necessary, as natural farming and permaculture show; winter cover crops, soil solarization and burning are alternatives.

title: Strip-till

definition.text: A minimum-tillage conservation system that tills only the narrow strip of soil that will hold the seed row, leaving the soil between rows untilled.

facts.text: It combines the soil drying and warming of conventional tillage with the soil protection of no-till.
Each strip-tilled row is usually about eight to ten inches wide.
Also called zone tillage, it breaks up plough pans under the row, helps warm the soil, prepares a seedbed and improves internal drainage.
Breaking the crust lets air in and speeds organic matter decay, yet a two-year study found no change in soil organic carbon or extractable phosphorus.
Fertilizer can be placed directly in the seed row during strip-tilling, cutting the amount needed and putting it closer to the roots.
Combined implements can cut field trips to two or even one, saving time and fuel and reducing compaction.
It conserves more moisture than intensive tillage, though sometimes less than no-till, and erosion is light by comparison with intensive tillage.
At a low-phosphorus site strip-till yielded 43.5 bushels/acre (2,925.5 kg/ha) against 41.5 bu/a (2,791 kg/ha) under no-till; yields match intensive tillage without its cost.

conflicts.text: Zone tillage produces a tilled strip approximately five inches wide.
conflicts.note: Tillage#Zone tillage treats zone and strip tillage as one practice; the Strip-till article gives eight to ten inches per row.

notes: Folds in Tillage#Zone tillage (zone or strip tillage). Zone tillage is said to be used on more than 36% of US farmland (S:abec1b5421cf); left out pending verification.

title: Minimum tillage

definition.text: A soil conservation system that keeps soil manipulation to the minimum a crop needs, without turning the soil over.

facts.text: Primary tillage is avoided entirely, and secondary tillage is practised only to a small extent.
It includes minimum furrowing, organic fertilizer, biological pest control and minimal use of chemicals.
Some minimum or low-till methods mix tilled and untilled approaches, for example shallow disc harrowing without ploughing, or strip tillage.

notes: Crawled page that no chapter's dossier lists; drafted here. Close to Reduced tillage: merge if selection prefers.

title: Vertical tillage

definition.text: A set of tillage principles that, like conservation agriculture, aims to improve soil health, raise infiltration and reduce erosion and compaction.

facts.text: It avoids inverting the soil and keeps residue on the surface, using small forward-facing discs that slice residue for faster decomposition.
It often adds a deep ripping tool to break hard pans and compaction left by traditional implements and heavy machinery such as combine harvesters.
Proponents class it with no-till and conservation agriculture; detractors say its vigorous soil movement excludes it, which matters for US payments that promote no-till.
What counts as vertical tillage varies considerably, even among its proponents.

contested_note: Proponents and detractors disagree over whether vertical tillage belongs with no-till and conservation agriculture, and its definition varies.
notes: Two lead sentences carry WHO? tags (S:1abe3c3cd703, S:ad91351b9ad1): the sides of the dispute are unattributed.

title: Contour plowing

definition.text: Ploughing or planting across a slope along its elevation contour lines, also called contour farming.

facts.text: The level furrows run across the slope rather than down it, forming water breaks that reduce rills and gullies in heavy rain and give water time to soak in.
It also helps prevent tillage erosion, the movement of soil by tilling itself.
It reduces fertilizer loss, power use, time and machine wear while raising yields; demonstrations showed row-crop gains of up to 50% under ideal conditions, with 5 to 10% common.
The Phoenicians developed contour farming and spread it around the Mediterranean, but the Romans preferred straight furrows, which became standard.
The US Soil Conservation Service, set up in 1935 during the Dust Bowl, promoted it; by 1938 such techniques had cut soil loss by 65% despite continuing drought.
It works only on slopes of 2% to 10% and below a certain rainfall; steeper or wetter land adds strip cropping, and terraces and cover crops make it more effective.
In the similar practice of contour bunding, stones are placed along the contours of slopes.

conflicts.text: Contour plowing can increase crop yields by 10 to 50 percent.
conflicts.note: Soil conservation#Contour ploughing (citing 1943); the Contour plowing article gives up to 50% under ideal conditions, with 5 to 10% common.

notes: Soil conservation#Contour ploughing (soil-conservation chapter) adds S:cb420d88cd08: Phoenicians on slopes of two to ten percent; not drafted twice.

image.caption: Unknown author Unknown author, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

definition.text: P. A. Yeomans' system of planning farm landscapes around the natural flow of water to make the best use of their water resources.

facts.text: The keyline is the contour through the keypoint, where a valley floor suddenly steepens; cultivating parallel to it drifts runoff away from the valley centre.
Ordinary contour ploughing drifts off contour too, sending runoff off ridges into valleys; keyline cultivation delays runoff concentration and gives water more time to infiltrate.
Its Keyline Scale of Permanence orders farm elements from landshape and water supply through roads and structures to fences.
Philipp Gerhardt's Seepage Line System replaces fixed keylines with custom contour ditches, and trials in Germany show it reduces surface runoff.

title: Optimum water content for tillage

definition.text: The soil moisture content at which tillage breaks the soil into the largest number of small aggregates.

facts.text: Tilling wetter or drier than the optimum damages structure by producing large clods and raises the readily dispersible clay content.
It can be related to the water content at the lower plastic limit; for several soils the optimum equals 0.9 times the plastic limit.
That link has limits: the plastic limit is measured on moulded rather than undisturbed soil, and many sandy soils have no plastic limit.
Many clay soils drain so slowly that they stay wetter than the plastic limit unless plant roots draw the water out; friability, the tendency to crumble, peaks at the plastic limit.

notes: The page's Overview (S:98c2d97bec31, S:71d082806de7, S:6b3729ba4b7c) describes the compaction (Proctor) optimum, a different quantity, and claims maximum dry unit weight means no voids; not used.

definition.text: Land that can be ploughed and used to grow crops.

facts.text: In FAO statistics it means land under temporary crops, temporary meadows, market and kitchen gardens, and land fallow for less than five years; land abandoned by shifting cultivation is excluded.
The statistics record actual, not potential, use; Eurostat defines it as land ploughed or tilled regularly, generally under crop rotation.
In 2013 the world had 1.407 billion hectares of arable land out of 4.924 billion hectares used for agriculture.
Agricultural land that is not arable includes meadows and pastures and permanent crops such as orchards, vineyards and coffee plantations.
Land may be unfit for cultivation through lack of freshwater, stoniness, steepness, adverse climate, undrainable wetness or excess salts; clay content is a major factor in arability.
Such land can still be productive: about 59 percent of US non-federal pasture and unforested rangeland cannot be cultivated but is valuable for grazing.
Arable land is lost every year to desertification and human-induced erosion, and improper irrigation concentrates salts in the root zone.
Climate change may add arable land by thawing frozen ground.

title: Conversion to arable land

definition.text: Making land that cannot grow crops capable of cultivation.

facts.text: It may require irrigation canals, wells, desalination, fertilizer, pesticides, windbreaks or heated greenhouses, and is often prohibitively expensive.
On the rocky Aran Islands off Ireland, people spread a shallow layer of seaweed and sand to grow crops, though the islands still count as non-arable.
Slash-and-burn farming draws on nutrients in wood ash, but these are used up within a few years; terra preta soils were made fertile by adding charcoal.

notes: Aran Islands sentence S:748e838e9eeb carries a WHEN? tag.

definition.text: A crop rotation in which a field grows one set of crops in the first year, a different set in the second and lies fallow in the third.

facts.text: An estate's arable land was split into three fields: one sown in autumn with winter wheat or rye, one with peas, lentils or beans, and one left fallow.
Legumes fixed nitrogen that cereals depleted, and livestock grazing the weedy fallow fertilized it with their excrement.
Each field was cropped two years in three, against half the land lying fallow under the older two-field system.
First used in China in the Eastern Zhou period, it spread in Europe from the 9th to the 11th century alongside the moldboard plough, though summer-dry Mediterranean lands suited it less.

title: Crop residue

definition.text: The stalks, stubble, leaves and other plant material left in a field after harvest.

facts.text: Farmers once treated residue as trash, but keeping more than 50% of it on the surface benefits soil health, nutrient cycling, erosion control and microbial activity.
Surface residue softens the impact of raindrops that break up soil particles, reducing splash and sheet erosion.
Covering the surface, it cuts evaporation, lowers surface soil temperature and reduces wind effects.
Decaying residue opens routes for water to soak in quickly, reducing the need for supplemental irrigation.
Residue cover defines tillage systems: under 15% for intensive, 15 to 30% for reduced and at least 30% for conservation tillage.
Leaving residues to decay returns their stored potassium to the soil.
Its nutrients are released slowly: by the next year cereal straw releases about 10 to 15 per cent of its nutrients and pea residue about 35 percent.
Residue with over 1.5 per cent nitrogen releases it quickly, but below 1.2 per cent microbes decomposing it immobilize soil nitrogen.

notes: Re-anchored on the Crop residue article in the gap-fill pass.

title: Controlled traffic farming

definition.text: A management system that confines all machinery loads to the smallest possible area of permanent traffic lanes, to limit soil damage from heavy or repeated passes.

facts.text: Random traffic compacts about 75% of a field in one season and all of it by the second, while a proper system cuts tracking to 15%, always in the same place.
It needs matched implement widths and wheel track widths, and machines kept in the same lanes every year, most easily with RTK satellite guidance and auto-steer accurate to about ± 2 cm.
Untracked soil gains porosity, infiltration and drainage, with less erosion and waterlogging and better rooting; most adopters till little or not at all because structure no longer needs repair.
Compacted soils can take more than 5 years to recover; drawbacks of the system are a high initial investment and the need for GPS guidance and adapted machines.

definition.text: Ploughing deeper than 50 cm, compared with ordinary ploughing that rarely goes below 20 cm.

facts.text: Its purpose is to change the soil's water retention over the long term.
In a 35-year test, deep-ploughed plots averaged 3,138 kg of grain per hectare a year, 10% more than the 2,858 kg from unploughed plots.
In soils such as Podzols it can break up a hardpan and help release nutrients, and it is sometimes recommended before planting vineyards.
Farming is moving away from ploughing, especially deep ploughing, to save topsoil and organic matter, though a 35-year study found no-ploughing does not conserve ground moisture.

definition.text: A harrow whose cutting edges are rows of concave metal discs set at an angle, used to till soil and chop weeds or crop residue.

facts.text: Because the discs are concave and offset from the direction of travel, they repeatedly slice the ground and loosen and lift the soil they cut.
Heavy primary disc harrows of 120 to 454 kg per disc break virgin land and work residue into the topsoil, speeding its decay; lighter secondary ones break clods into a seedbed.
It is the preferred way to work agricultural lime and gypsum into soil, reaching a 50/50 mix that reduces topsoil acid saturation.
Since lime does not move in the soil, this poses a critical challenge for zero-till farming.

definition.text: A seeding method in which the whole soil surface is tilled and crop residue mixed in, while some residue stays on the surface.

facts.text: It is done with a wide variety of cultivators and counts as conservation tillage in the United States.

definition.text: Deliberately setting fire to the straw stubble left after harvesting grains such as rice and wheat.

facts.text: It clears fields quickly and cheaply, helps combat pests and weeds, and can reduce nitrogen tie-up.
It wastes nutrients, and prolonged burning kills beneficial soil microflora and fauna, reducing organic matter and upsetting the carbon–nitrogen balance.
Its smoke spreads particulate pollution, linked to lung cancer, respiratory infections and harm to people with chronic lung disease.
It is illegal in India and Pakistan but weakly enforced, and has effectively been banned in the United Kingdom since 1993.
Spraying an enzyme that decomposes stubble into fertiliser improves the soil and avoids air pollution.
Residues can go into particle board or biofuel, though removing them can still cause erosion and nutrient loss.

definition.text: Leaving stubble or crop residue in place on the land as a surface cover during a fallow period.

facts.text: It can prevent soil erosion by wind or water and conserve soil moisture.

definition.text: A conservation tillage system that builds ridges or beds for the seed zone and keeps fixed traffic lanes.

facts.text: It is one of the conservation tillage practices, with no-till, in-row subsoiling and strip-till, that aim to keep 30% or more of the surface under crop residue.
Ridges allow the seed zone to dry and warm faster, give some weed control and reduce saturation after heavy rain; fixed travel lanes reduce overall compaction.
Poorly drained fields benefit greatly from ridging or bedding because the sensitive seedling root zone stays aerobic when wet; controlled-traffic lanes greatly reduce compaction.

definition.text: How tillage began with small-grain farmers and spread, from the ard and animal traction to the moldboard plough and powerful tractors.

facts.text: Tillage began with small-grain farmers of the Fertile Crescent, Europe and North Africa to make a fine, clean seedbed, give the crop a head start on weeds and stimulate mineralization of nutrients.
Centuries of this system caused excessive erosion, organic matter loss and nutrient depletion, especially around the Mediterranean.
Jethro Tull's 1731 book promoted row seeding with a seed drill and intensive tillage; he believed pulverized soil particles fed plants and grew wheat 13 years without manure by mining soil nutrients.
Pre-Columbian American farmers used no full-field tillage, instead direct seeding with planting sticks or hoeing small hills, and intercropped corn, beans and squash.

definition.text: Estimating the share of the soil surface still covered by crop residue after a sequence of tillage operations by multiplying each tool's remaining fraction.

facts.text: Each pass of a tillage tool buries some residue, so surface cover shrinks; when passes follow one another, remaining cover is estimated by multiplication.
Example: 80% cover after corn, then chisel (70%), tandem disk (45%), field cultivator and planter (75%) leaves about 19%; dropping the disk leaves 42%.
After corn or cereals a moldboard plough leaves 0-10% residue, twisted-point chisel 50-70%, tandem finishing disk 30-60%, field cultivator 60-90% and a row-crop planter 85-95%.
Speed, depth and soil moisture affect the amounts, and cover also depends on surface roughness and soil loosening.

definition.text: Tilling soil after frost has entered it but before it has penetrated more than about 2 inches (5 cm).

facts.text: Water moves up to the freezing front and the soil beneath dries; the frozen layer supports equipment, so compaction is reduced.
The rough surface favours water infiltration and prevents runoff; livestock farms can use it to incorporate or inject manure in winter.
Recent research in Nebraska and Australia indicates occasional tillage does not harm soil health; purposes include weed or insect control, incorporating immobile amendments and compaction relief.
It should be rare (once every 5-10 years) with tools that leave residue, because any tillage can destroy structure built by years of no-till.
